title: Quality assurance
blurb: Outline the purpose of quality assurance: independent, process-focused checks that give confidence quality standards will be met.
question: Halfway through building a flood barrier, the sponsor asks for independent confidence that the contractor's welding and inspection procedures are being followed and will produce a barrier that meets the required standards. Which quality activity provides this, and how does it differ from quality control?

teach.h: Confidence that the way we work will deliver quality
teach.body: The purpose of quality assurance is to provide confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards. It does this by evaluating performance and checking that the agreed processes and standards are actually being followed. In plain English: quality assurance looks at HOW the work is being done, so the sponsor and stakeholders can trust that good outputs will result. It is process-focused, preventive and ideally independent of the delivery team.

rows.label: Asks
values: Are we working the right way?

teach.caption: The single most tested contrast in this topic. Process = assurance. Product = control.

teach.body: Process: assurance examines methods, procedures and standards, not individual deliverables. Prevention: by spotting a process that is not being followed, it stops defects before they are made. Independence: it is ideally done by people outside the delivery team, such as the PMO or auditors, so the verdict is objective and stakeholders can rely on it.

root.label: Quality assurance
root.sub: ideally independent of the delivery team

teach.body: On the Seaview flood barrier, a reviewer from the PMO visits the site each month. She checks that welders hold current certificates, that the agreed welding procedure (including pre-heating) is followed on every shift, and that inspection records are kept as the quality plan requires. She finds the night shift skipping pre-heating. The procedure is enforced before any faulty welds are made. That is assurance. Separately, inspectors X-ray finished welds: that is quality control.

teach.text: The exam swaps these two constantly. If the stem talks about inspecting, measuring or testing a deliverable, that is quality CONTROL. If it talks about checking procedures are followed, auditing the process, or giving confidence, that is quality ASSURANCE. A handy hook: assurance ASSURES people; control CONTROLS products.

teach.note: Ask: is it looking at the way the work is done, or at the thing that was made?

items: Purpose of quality assurance: to provide confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards.
It evaluates performance and checks that agreed processes and standards are followed.
Process-focused and preventive; ideally independent of the delivery team (e.g. PMO, auditors).
Quality control is the opposite side: product-focused, inspecting and testing outputs, detecting defects.

summary: You can now outline the purpose of quality assurance: giving confidence that quality standards will be met by independently checking that agreed processes are followed. You can also separate it cleanly from quality control, which inspects and tests the outputs themselves.

A.q: What is the main purpose of quality assurance on a project?
options: To inspect outputs and reject faulty ones
To give confidence quality standards will be met
To set the acceptance criteria for outputs
To decide whether the project should go ahead or stop
A.why: Quality assurance provides confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards, by checking agreed processes are followed.

whyNot.0: Inspecting and rejecting outputs is quality control.
whyNot.2: Setting acceptance criteria is quality planning.
whyNot.3: Deciding whether to continue happens at a decision gate.

A.q: Which description best fits quality assurance?
options: Process-focused and preventive
Product-focused and detective
Benefits-focused and reactive
Schedule-focused and corrective
A.why: Quality assurance examines processes and aims to prevent defects by making sure the agreed way of working is followed.

whyNot.1: Product-focused and detective describes quality control.
whyNot.2: Benefits are assessed in a benefits review, not by quality assurance.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance is not about the schedule, and it aims to prevent rather than correct.

A.q: Who would ideally carry out quality assurance on a project?
options: The team member who built the output
Someone independent of the delivery team
The end users once the project has closed
The supplier who produced the output
A.why: Quality assurance is ideally independent of the delivery team, for example the PMO or auditors, so its findings are objective.

whyNot.0: The person who built the output is not independent of the work.
whyNot.2: Assurance happens during the project, not after closure.
whyNot.3: The supplier is part of delivery, so it is not independent.

B.q: A PMO reviewer checks that a software team follows its agreed code review procedure on every release. Is this quality assurance or quality control?
options: Control, as it tests the software product
Control, as it measures each output
Assurance, as it inspects the final product
Assurance, as it examines the process used
B.why: Checking that an agreed procedure is being followed examines the process, so it is quality assurance.

whyNot.0: No software is being tested; the reviewer is looking at the procedure.
whyNot.1: No output is being measured; the focus is on how the work is done.
whyNot.2: It is assurance, but for the wrong reason: assurance looks at the process, not the product.

B.q: Why is it preferable for quality assurance to be independent of the delivery team?
options: So the team no longer needs to test outputs
So that decision gates can be skipped
So the review of processes is objective
So the sponsor need not approve the plan
B.why: Independence makes the assessment of processes objective and unbiased, so stakeholders can rely on it.

whyNot.0: Testing outputs (quality control) is still needed alongside assurance.
whyNot.1: Decision gates are governance controls; assurance does not replace them.
whyNot.3: The sponsor still approves the plan; assurance does not change that.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are typical quality assurance activities?
1. An audit of whether procedures are followed
2. Load-testing a finished bridge beam
3. A peer review of the agreed design method
4. Measuring finished parts against tolerances
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Audits of procedures and peer reviews of methods both examine the process, so both are quality assurance.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is quality control: it tests a finished product.
whyNot.2: Both statements describe quality control: testing and measuring outputs.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is quality control: it measures finished parts.

C.q: Midway through delivery, a sponsor wants confidence that the construction methods in use will produce a building that meets the required standards. Which activity provides this?
options: Quality control
Quality planning
Post-project review
Quality assurance
C.why: Giving confidence that the processes in use will meet the standards is the purpose of quality assurance.

whyNot.0: Quality control inspects and tests the outputs already produced, not the methods.
whyNot.1: Quality planning set the standards before the work; it does not check methods during it.
whyNot.2: A post-project review captures lessons at closure; it cannot give confidence midway.

C.q: An independent review finds a key procedure is not being followed consistently, although no defects have appeared yet. What does this show about quality assurance?
options: It is preventive: it finds process gaps early
It is detective: it finds defects in outputs
It is only useful once defects have appeared
It removes the need for quality control checks
C.why: By finding a process gap before defects occur, quality assurance prevents problems rather than detecting them afterwards.

whyNot.1: No defects were found; the review looked at the process, which is preventive.
whyNot.2: The value here is that it acted before any defects appeared.
whyNot.3: Quality control is still needed to verify the outputs themselves.

C.q: Which statement about quality assurance and quality control is correct?
options: Assurance tests outputs; control audits processes
Assurance is for linear projects; control iterative
Assurance checks processes; control tests outputs
Assurance takes place only after handover to users
C.why: Assurance checks that agreed processes are followed; control inspects and tests the outputs.

whyNot.0: This reverses them: control tests outputs and assurance checks processes.
whyNot.1: Both apply in any life cycle, linear or iterative.
whyNot.3: Assurance happens during the project, while there is still time to act.

reteach.title: Think of building a music festival stage
reteach.question: A festival is putting up a huge main stage. One person checks the crew are following the agreed rigging procedure; another load-tests the finished stage. Which one is doing quality assurance?

blocks.h: Watching the method vs testing the result
blocks.body: The festival's safety officer does not work for the staging company. She walks the site checking that riggers are trained, that the agreed build sequence is followed and that every bolt torque is being recorded as the procedure says. That is quality assurance: an independent check on the process, so the organisers can be confident. The engineer who load-tests the finished stage before the gates open is doing quality control: testing the product.

blocks.text: Being independent does not make something assurance on its own. An independent inspector testing a product is still doing quality control. Assurance is about the process.

explain.body: Quality assurance exists to give the sponsor and stakeholders confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards.

test.q: Complete the statement: the purpose of quality assurance is to provide ______ that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards.
options: confidence
funding
acceptance
authority
test.why: Quality assurance provides confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards.

whyNot.1: Funding is secured by the sponsor through the business case, not by assurance.
whyNot.2: Acceptance of outputs follows quality control against acceptance criteria.
whyNot.3: Authority comes from governance and the sponsor, not from quality assurance.

explain.body: Quality assurance examines the methods, procedures and standards being used, not individual deliverables. Good processes, followed consistently, produce good outputs.

test.q: Which of the following does quality assurance mainly examine?
options: The finished deliverables
The processes being used
The benefits being realised
The budget being spent
test.why: Quality assurance is process-focused: it checks the agreed processes and standards are being followed.

whyNot.0: Finished deliverables are examined by quality control.
whyNot.2: Benefits are assessed in a benefits review.
whyNot.3: Spend is tracked through cost control and progress reporting.

explain.body: Because it checks the process while work is under way, assurance can stop defects before they are made. Quality control, by contrast, detects defects after outputs exist.

test.q: A review spots that welders on one shift skip a pre-heating step, and the procedure is enforced before any faulty welds are made. Which characteristic does this best illustrate?
options: Detection of defects by final inspection
Gold plating of the welding process
Prevention through checking the process
Acceptance of outputs by end users
test.why: Checking the process and fixing it before defects occur is the preventive nature of quality assurance.

whyNot.0: No outputs were inspected and no defects were found; the process was checked.
whyNot.1: Gold plating means adding unrequested extras; nothing extra was added.
whyNot.3: End users were not involved; this was a check on the working process.

explain.body: Assurance is most credible when done by people outside the delivery team: the PMO, internal or external auditors, or peer reviewers from another team.

test.q: Which of the following would be LEAST suitable to provide independent quality assurance?
options: The project management office
An internal audit team
An external auditor
The team doing the work
test.why: The delivery team cannot be independent of its own work, so it is least suitable for independent assurance.

whyNot.0: The PMO commonly provides independent assurance to projects.
whyNot.1: Internal audit is independent of the delivery team.
whyNot.2: An external auditor is fully independent of the project.
